instruction: How do I declare a typed list in Graphoid?
output:
# Use single-parameter type constraints on built-in collections
list<num> scores = [95, 87, 92]
print(scores)        # [95, 87, 92]
print(scores.length())  # 3

# Adding a non-num value will raise a runtime error
# scores.append!("hello")  # Error: Cannot append string to list<num>

instruction: What type constraints are allowed in Graphoid?
output:
# Single-parameter, runtime-checked constraints on built-in collections ONLY
list<num> numbers = [1, 2, 3]       # list of numbers
list<string> names = ["Alice", "Bob"]  # list of strings
list<bool> flags = [true, false]     # list of booleans

# Type is optional — inference is preferred
items = [1, 2, 3]  # same as list<num>, but inferred

# FORBIDDEN:
# list<list<num>> matrix = []    # nested constraints
# hash<string, num> data = {}    # multiple params
# fn process<T>(x: T) { }       # generic functions

instruction: When should I use explicit type constraints vs type inference in Graphoid?
output:
# Prefer type inference (idiomatic)
name = "Alice"           # inferred as string
scores = [95, 87, 92]    # inferred as list
config = {"port": 8080}  # inferred as map

# Use explicit types when you want runtime enforcement
list<num> measurements = []
# Now any non-number append will be caught:
measurements.append!(42)     # ok
# measurements.append!("x")  # Error at runtime

# Rule of thumb: explicit types for public API boundaries,
# inference for local variables

instruction: Can I create a typed tree or graph in Graphoid?
output:
# Yes — single-parameter type constraints work on built-in collections

# Tree node value type
tree<num> numbers = tree{}
numbers.add_node("root", 100)
numbers.add_node("left", 50)
numbers.add_edge("root", "left")
print(numbers.node_count())  # 2

# Graph node value type
graph<string> names = graph { type: :directed }
names.add_node("n1", "Alice")
print(names.node_count())  # 1

# list<num> is the most common
list<num> scores = [95, 87, 92]
print(scores)  # [95, 87, 92]
